newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl tries to regain initiative on German reforms.
newsitem.headline: Kohl tries to regain initiative on German reforms.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl tried on Friday to regain the initiative on key reforms after a week of protests from miners and building workers fearful they may be next to join record post-war dole queues.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel unveiled draft legislation for sweeping tax cuts, and Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) huddled to agree a party line on remodelling the state pensions scheme.
Kohl, who defused a week-long dispute over coal subsidies on Thursday, called on the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) to return to negotiations to seek a compromise on tax cuts.
"The government has made its offer. The SPD must do the rest," Kohl said at his party headquarters.
Kohl said he was still waiting for the SPD to offer worthwhile proposals. "Apart from a barrage of criticism, we have heard very little from the other side," he said.

The government wants its tax and pensions reforms to revitalise Germany's social market economy by capping the cost of generous welfare provision and creating better conditions for investment to cut unemployment at 4.7 million.

They are also aimed at strenghtening Bonn's attempt to join European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999. But the belt-tightening required to meet that goal has led to a spate of labour protests.

Construction workers, unimpressed by government plans to plough 25 billion marks ($14.7 billion) into building investment, rounded off five days of protests in Berlin against mass unemployment on Friday by storming the Reichstag -- Germany's past and future parliament.

Unemployment in the construction sector -- which embarked on a building frenzy after German unification in 1990 but is now in a slump -- is estimated at 400,000. The workers blame "wage dumping" by cheap foreign labour.
"Sometime the bomb will explode. My God, we don't want to be violent but sometimes it comes down to that," one builder said.
Dieter Schulte, head of the Trade Union Federation (DGB), blamed the government for supporting "modern-day slavery" by allowing foreign workers to undercut wages.
Waigel hopes to repeat the job-creating growth formula found by North American and British governments in recent years by cutting 30 billion marks in income and corporate taxes.

"With these proposals, fiscal policy is showing the way to more growth and jobs in our country," he told reporters. The reform could boost economic growth by half a percentage point a year and investment by 1.5 points, he said.

But the SPD, which quit cross-party tax talks a week ago in solidarity with protesting coal workers, called on the government to produce new proposals which would boost the income of ordinary workers and stimulate domestic demand.
Party leader Oskar Lafontaine said most Germans could not understand Kohl's calls for wage restraint going hand-in-hand with tax cuts worth 20,000 or 30,000 marks a year for the rich.
"That is more than these poor people fighting for their jobs earn in a whole year," Lafontaine told parliament in an unemployment debate.

No date has been set for a new round of cross-party talks on tax. Failure to reach a deal by the coalition's Easter deadline would condemn the measures to parliamentary trench warfare which could drag into the 1998 election campaign. The SPD can veto tax measures in the upper house.
But the government may not have that long to put its house in order, and another top economist joined a chorus of doubters saying Germany cannot make the grade for EMU.
Heiner Flassbeck, chief economist at the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW), told Reuters Financial Television: "In our opinion the government won't meet the fiscal criteria this year."

The Maastricht treaty sets a budget deficit limit of three percent of GDP this year, and a public debt ceiling of 60 percent of GDP. If countries miss, the numbers should be on track towards those reference values, the treaty says.

Flassbeck said he expected the budget deficit to be 3.5 percent of GDP. A European Union source in Brussels also said Germany's national debt would rise rather than fall this year. According to Germany's convergence plan, the debt will rise to 61.5 percent of GDP from 60.7 percent in 1996.
Germany faces a difficult choice of agreeing to a generous reading of Maastricht, which could let countries such as Italy into EMU at the start, or having to delay the euro project.
But a former central banker dismissed fears that a delay would send the German mark "shooting through the roof".
"I believe that in the event of a postponement the effect on financial markets would be very limited," Gerd Haeusler, who is now on the board of Dresdner Bank AG, told Reuters.
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, however, said in Copenhagen that now was not the time to be discussing a delay in Europe's single currency.

"I hope that Germany will be able to participate...it is not the right time to discuss this, let's wait until spring 1998," he said. European leaders are due then to decide on the 'ins' and 'outs' of the single currency. ($ = 1.704 German Marks)
